transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Hello, come in. Hi Mia, I'm Dr Lindqvist. And you're Dad?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Yes, I'm Raj.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: What's been going on?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Her eczema's flared up really badly. She's scratching all night and none of us are sleeping.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: How long has this flare been going on?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: About a month. No, actually, she started scratching after half-term, so two weeks.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Two weeks, then. Where is it worst?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: The backs of her knees and the insides of her elbows. Her right elbow's the worst.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It's so itchy.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: I bet it is, Mia. Does it ever weep, or get crusty or yellow?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: No, just red and dry and scratched.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any blisters, or painful sores that look like little punched-out holes?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Has she had any fevers or been unwell?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: No, she's fine otherwise.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: What are you using on it?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Epaderm, but honestly only once a day. And some hydrocortisone cream from the chemist.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: How strong is the hydrocortisone?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: One percent.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Is she on any other medicines? Any allergies?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: No and no.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Does anyone in the family have eczema, asthma or hay fever?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: I've got hay fever. Her big sister has asthma.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: And has Mia ever had asthma or wheezing?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: No, never.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any pets at home?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: A cat. She's had the cat all her life, though.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Has anything changed? New soaps, bubble bath, washing powder?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: She's started having bubble baths at her mum's.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: That could be a trigger. Mia, can I look at your arms and legs? Thank you. There are dry, red, scratched patches in both elbow creases and behind both knees. The right elbow crease is the worst. There's no weeping, crusting or blisters, so no sign of infection.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: That's good.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: This is a moderate flare. I'd like to use a stronger steroid cream for a short time. It's called clobetasone butyrate, 0.05 percent. Put it on the red patches on her body once a day for seven days, then go back to the hydrocortisone for a few days if needed.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Is it safe?

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Yes, for a short course it's safe. Use a fingertip unit, that's a line of cream from the tip of your finger to the first crease, for an area the size of two adult hands.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: The most important thing is the moisturiser. Use the Epaderm three or four times a day, lots of it, at least a 500 gram tub every two weeks. Use it instead of soap, and stop the bubble baths.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Okay. I'll talk to her mum.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: I'd like to see her again in two weeks.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: If she gets painful sores, blisters or punched-out spots, especially with a fever or feeling unwell, that can be a herpes infection in eczema. Get her seen the same day.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Okay, thank you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Bye!

reference_note.presenting_complaint: Flare of atopic eczema for 2 weeks.
reference_note.history: Flare for 2 weeks (father initially said a month, then corrected), worst in the flexures, particularly the right elbow. Nocturnal itch disturbing sleep. No weeping, crusting, blisters or punched-out lesions. Systemically well. Recently started bubble baths. Using Epaderm once daily and hydrocortisone 1%. No personal history of asthma or wheeze. Father has hay fever; sister has asthma. Pet cat at home.
reference_note.medications_allergies: Epaderm emollient. Hydrocortisone 1% cream (over the counter). No known drug allergies.
reference_note.examination: Dry, erythematous, excoriated patches in both antecubital and both popliteal fossae, most severe in the right antecubital fossa. No weeping, crusting or vesicles.
reference_note.impression: Moderate flare of atopic eczema; no signs of infection. Possible trigger: bubble baths.
reference_note.plan: Clobetasone butyrate 0.05% once daily to inflamed areas on the body for 7 days, then hydrocortisone 1% if needed. Fingertip units explained. Epaderm 3–4 times daily and as a soap substitute (at least 500 g every 2 weeks). Stop bubble baths. Review in 2 weeks.
reference_note.safety_netting: Seek same-day review if painful sores, blisters or punched-out lesions, especially with fever or feeling unwell (possible eczema herpeticum).

mutations.seeded_rationale: The side of the worst patch matters little in symmetrical flexural eczema.

mutations.seeded_rationale: Clobetasol is a very potent steroid, not moderate; in a child it increases the risk of skin thinning and adrenal suppression, and the names are easily confused at dispensing.
mutations.description: Moderate steroid swapped for a very potent one
